summary: Builds on RFCs 3689 and 3690, which describe requirements for an Emergency Telecommunications Service, including an Internet Emergency Preparedness Service. Some such services need call preemption or queuing, and they need call admission control. This informational memo discusses how to implement those capabilities for real-time services in the IP suite.

plainLanguage.summary: In an emergency, important calls should get through first, like an ambulance going ahead of other cars. This memo explains how internet phone and video services can make room for them.

questions: how to prioritize emergency calls on ip networks
what is an emergency telecommunications service
what is the sip resource priority header
subtitle: How SIP, RSVP and Differentiated Services can be combined so authorized emergency calls get through first on IP networks.

tldr.problem: In a crisis, authorized users need an elevated probability that their real-time calls (voice and video) complete, even when the network is congested. IP networks had no agreed way to give them that.
tldr.mechanism: Callers mark each call with a precedence level in the SIP Resource-Priority header, and the network admits bandwidth with RSVP policy that can preempt lower-precedence sessions. Voice data is forwarded with the Expedited Forwarding PHB, and a preempted call is ended with a SIP BYE carrying a preemption reason.
tldr.outcome: The RFC is Informational and is built entirely from existing specifications. It is updated by a later RFC.

today: RFC 4542 is Informational and is updated by RFC 5865. It describes how to combine existing specifications and does not define a new protocol.

sections.title: The Emergency Service Problem
sections.content:
RFC 3689 and RFC 3690 set out requirements for an Emergency Telecommunications Service (ETS), of which an Internet Emergency Preference Service (IEPS) would be a part. Some such services need call preemption, others need call queuing or other mechanisms. The key requirement is to guarantee an elevated probability of call completion to an authorized user in time of crisis.

IEPS needs a Call Admission Control (CAC) procedure and a Per Hop Behavior (PHB) for the data. The RFC says this is appropriate to any service that might use H.323 or SIP to set up real-time sessions, including but not limited to voice and video, though most of its examples are voice.

The document focuses on the US Government and NATO, because it builds on the Multi-Level Precedence and Preemption (MLPP) and Government Emergency Telecommunication Service (GETS) standards, and says the architecture is applicable beyond these organizations.
sections.plainLanguage: When something terrible happens, everyone calls at once and the lines fill up. This memo is a plan so the most important calls still go through.

sections.title: MLPP, GETS and Call Admission
sections.content:
MLPP is an existing ITU-T, NATO and US Department of Defense telephone architecture in which more important calls override less important ones when congestion occurs. The caller picks a precedence level when the call starts and it cannot change during the call. If none is chosen, the call is treated as routine. When a trunk group (or, in IP, an interface) reaches a utilization threshold, the system preempts existing lower-precedence calls to make room, and preempted parties are notified by a preemption tone.

GETS is a similar US civilian service. It does not use preemption, but reserves bandwidth or queues calls, and it has only two levels, Routine and Priority.

Call admission control checks bandwidth thresholds and whether the caller is permitted to use a circuit. For emergency service it may also use other networks, preempt other calls, hold a call until others finish, or apply different bandwidth thresholds. The RFC's list of desired characteristics is: precedence marking of each call, a call admission and preemption policy, a bandwidth admission policy, authentication and authorization, voice handling characteristics, and a defined user interface.
sections.plainLanguage: Every call gets a label saying how important it is, and the label cannot change once the call starts. If the phone lines are full, a more important call can bump a less important one off, and the bumped person hears a special tone.

sections.title: Call Admission and Preemption with SIP
sections.content:
Call setup carries the precedence in the SIP Resource-Priority header from RFC 4412, written Resource Priority: namespace.priority level. The namespace names the domain of significance, which allows service level agreements to limit who may get preferential treatment. A phone that does not support the namespace can ignore the request.

For the DSN the levels, in descending order, are dsn.flash-override, dsn.flash, dsn.immediate, dsn.priority and dsn.routine. The DRSN adds drsn.flash-override-override above them. The first-hop SIP proxy typically compares the requested level with the requester's authorization profile.

When a call is preempted, the SIP BYE request is used to end it, carrying the Reason header for preemption from RFC 4411, so all SIP nodes learn that a preemption occurred, whether at an endpoint or in a congested router. In the RFC's example, Alice calls Bob at Routine, then Carol calls Bob at Immediate. Bob's user agent compares the Resource-Priority values, ends Alice's call and answers Carol.
sections.plainLanguage: When Carol's more important call arrives, Bob's phone looks at both labels, hangs up on Alice's less important call, and tells her why. Then it picks up Carol.

sections.title: Voice Handling in the Data Path
sections.content:
In the data path the architecture is Differentiated Services (RFC 2475), which flags a stream with a DSCP and applies a Per Hop Behavior. The Expedited Forwarding PHB describes the fundamental needs of voice and video: enough bandwidth is dedicated to real-time traffic that variation in delay and loss stay minimal. Where bandwidth is heavily over-provisioned there may be no remaining concern, while constrained places may need a priority queue.

If a priority queue is used it can be abused, so traffic placed into it must be policed. The RFC points at first-hop routers and at points where converging streams could congest a link. The application should generate traffic at a rate suited to its codec, and with bandwidth-aware admission control there should be minimal actual loss. Where loss does occur, the RFC prefers rejecting or preempting an entire call over spreading random loss across all calls.
sections.plainLanguage: Voice needs a smooth lane on the road with no traffic jams. The network keeps that lane for calls and checks that nobody sneaks extra cars into it.

sections.title: Bandwidth Admission with RSVP
sections.content:
Counting calls at an H.323 gatekeeper or a SIP proxy is only a short-term work-around, because it has no knowledge of routing. The recommended approach is explicit capacity admission supporting preemption, for example with the Resource Reservation Protocol (RSVP, RFC 2205), used together with SIP as described in RFC 3312.

RSVP sets up one-way reservations and keeps soft state: reservations are cleared automatically after an outage or routing change unless refreshed, and the default refresh period is 30 seconds. It is local to each device, so it can work when enabled at only some nodes. Backbones may carry RSVP through tunnels (RFC 2746, RFC 2207) or aggregate reservations (RFC 3175), copying the DSCP from the inner to the outer header. The DCLASS object (RFC 2996) carries the DSCP for the call's precedence.

RSVP's basic policy grants bandwidth when enough is free. Variable rate codecs may use statistical policies such as over-provisioning the admission limit or tracking average load. Policy decisions can come from a local or a remote policy server. If a flow is admitted beyond capacity, RSVP tears down one of the lowest-precedence sessions, and the application (SIP or H.323) disconnects its call with the reason code "bandwidth preemption".
sections.plainLanguage: Along the road, each router is asked to save a seat for the call. The saved seat has to be renewed every so often. If the road is full, a seat held by a less important call is given to the important one.

sections.title: Authorization, User Interface and Security
sections.content:
Any policy must be applied to an authenticated user, and the capabilities of an authenticated user may be treated as authorized. For bandwidth admission this uses RSVP cryptographic authentication (RFC 2747, RFC 3097), and SIP and H.323 also need AAA procedures.

The user interface, the chimes and tones heard by the user, should ideally stay the same as in the telephone network where they still apply, and indications should rely on positive signals rather than unreliable measurements.

The Security Considerations section is short. The capability is composed entirely of existing specifications, and a failure of authentication or authorization can cause a fundamental breakdown in communications. The RFC says the issues are internal to the component protocols and covered by their own security procedures.
sections.plainLanguage: Only people with the right pass may use the express lane, so the network has to check passes carefully. Callers should also hear the same familiar beeps they know from ordinary phones.
